svg.aria-label: Diagram: what Infrastructure Manager takes over from self-managed Terraform, the service account identity model that replaces the state bucket as the real access decision, the lock required to read state, the bounded revision history, and the abandon deletion path
svg.title: Infrastructure Manager: what it takes over, what it relocates, and the doors that open one way
svg.text: A managed service is a trade, not a saving
It removes some decisions and relocates others. The relocated ones are the surprises.
Taken over — post #25’s morning of work
It creates the Cloud Storage bucket and holds the
deployment metadata: logs, the configuration used,
the resource list, and the state file per revision.
Bucket settings, versioning, access and the backend
block all stop being decisions.
Locking is structural here, not something to configure.
Relocated — the question that remains
Infra Manager executes Terraform using the identity
of a service account — never the person who
triggered the deployment.
That account needs permissions for everything the
configuration deploys. A user needs only Service
Account User on it to run a deployment.
Post #25’s risk did not go away. It changed shape.
From “who can read this bucket” to “who can act as this account”. The first looks like storage and invites a
lock-down. The second is a line in an IAM policy that looks like nothing at all. Audit it just as hard.
Reading your own state is a transaction
The deployment must be locked to be able to
download the state file, and it arrives through a
signed URL rather than a bucket you browse.
lock → export-statefile → export-lock → unlock
Rehearse it before the night you need it.
Abandon is the one-way door
Deleting a deployment lets you keep the resources
it provisioned. A legitimate hand-off — and final.
After you delete the deployment, Infra Manager is not
able to identify or manage the resources kept.
Nothing marks them as orphaned. Name an owner.
The numbers worth knowing before you design around them
historical revisions per deployment — a debugging history, not a compliance archive.
characters of identifier — tighter than any naming budget in post #18, and you type it often.
Terraform input variables — a configuration near this is asking to be split.
mutating requests a minute per project per region — the first wall a busy pipeline meets.
A preview describes the actions to actuate a configuration, and provisions nothing.
Same instinct as post #21’s dry-run mode, and stronger: a preview is complete, where a dry-run policy sees only
the traffic that happens to arrive while it is running.
Managed services move risk from where you are looking to where you are not. Go and look at the new place.
